strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real bottleneck in VLA inference (>70% latency in LLM)
Sound empirical insight validated through comprehensive visualization: consecutive action frames exhibit high visual similarity, enabling effective temporal pruning
Comprehensive experimental setup: 4 LIBERO datasets, 40-50 repetitions per task, testing on two hardware platforms (A800, RTX 3090) with consistent speedup gains
Training-free approach with practical applicability to existing VLA models
Practical action-aware controller distinguishing fine-grained precision-critical operations from coarse-grained actions, effectively protecting task success
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and organized structure
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: restricted to simulation (LIBERO benchmark) with no real-world robot deployment; critical gap for robotics application

Incremental novelty: combines existing techniques (attention-based pruning, layer-wise importance, early-layer speculation) without introducing fundamentally new ideas; temporal consistency insight is not novel

Multiple ad-hoc design choices lack justification: (1) velocity-based frame sampling formula appears arbitrary with specific coefficients unexplained, (2) layer confidence score formulation (Eq. 6) lacks theoretical foundation, (3) exponential moving average learning rate β=0.2 has no sensitivity analysis
Modest speedup gains (1.46×) with marginal improvement over EfficientVLA (1.55×) given added complexity; speedup not dramatic relative to potential

Reproducibility concerns: many hyperparameters (K_G, K_D, K_base, τ, velocity thresholds) lack clear selection criteria; EfficientVLA re-implemented rather than using official code; no code availability mentioned

Incomplete experimental validation: (1) ablation study only on LIBERO-Spatial; (2) no ablation within static/dynamic pruning components; (3) no statistical significance testing for success rate claims; (4) design space exploration limited to single dataset (LIBERO-Object)
Misleading terminology: 'self-speculative' framing overstates connection to speculative decoding; method only uses early layer information without verification typical of speculative approaches

Assumptions under-validated: (1) temporal consistency across frames not analyzed for failure modes; (2) action granularity detection via velocity may not generalize across robot systems; (3) layer confidence metric assumption not empirically validated

Missing critical analysis: no failure case studies, no error analysis, no computational cost of pruning itself, no evaluation on VLA models beyond OpenVLA-OFT despite claiming to evaluate three models
Success rate improvements marginal in some cases (e.g., 98.2% vs 97.6%): within typical noise margins and not statistically validated

strengths: Well-identified VLA-specific insights with solid empirical validation: hierarchical attention patterns and spatial-temporal consistency (75-88% token overlap across frames) go beyond generic acceleration methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple LIBERO suites, two model architectures, real-world robot validation, and robustness studies on environmental perturbations
Training-free method with practical applicability to deployed models without fine-tuning
Thorough ablation studies and extended evaluation on different hardware platforms demonstrating reproducibility
Good presentation with clear figures, intuitive explanations, and extensive supplementary material
weaknesses: Speedup results do not outperform strongest baseline: EfficientVLA achieves 1.52× vs. our 1.46×; FastV (1.44×) and DivPrune (1.46×) are comparable, making speedup advantage unclear
Success rate degradation overstated as 'negligible': LIBERO-Long shows 1.1% drop (94.5→93.4%), and real-world tasks show 1-3% degradation, which is significant for safety-critical robotics

Excessive hyperparameter complexity with heuristic design choices: constants b=7, k=-1 in frame sampling formula, layer selection (15, 32), pruning interval T=5, velocity thresholds—most lack theoretical justification and appear over-fit to specific scenarios

Limited novelty: token pruning via attention, entropy-based layer weighting (from Zhang et al. 2025), and rank-based importance are established techniques; main contribution is combining them with velocity-based action classification
Computational overhead (4.5%) is substantial relative to speedup gains (~3-4% over some baselines), and overhead analysis assumes entropy patterns remain consistent across different tasks
Spatial-temporal consistency assumption not fully robust: 12-25% of important tokens change between frames, with no analysis of failure modes when this assumption breaks down

strengths: Well-motivated approach with clear empirical insights about spatial-temporal consistency (75-88% token recall across consecutive steps), convincingly demonstrated in Figure 3
Comprehensive three-level pruning design combining global context reuse, dynamic token detection, and local attention from early layers with principled entropy-based layer weighting

Extensive and rigorous evaluation including multiple architectures (OpenVLA-OFT, π0), multiple benchmarks (LIBERO variants), real-world robot validation (1.70× speedup), and thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3, Figure 8)

Practical training-free method with detailed reproducibility information (Algorithm 1, hyperparameters, implementation details) and minimal success rate degradation (<0.7% on LIBERO, <3% on real-world)
Real-world validation on actual robot platform demonstrating generalization across different robot kinematics (Franka Panda, Flexiv Rizon, WidowX in appendix A.1.4)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (attention-based pruning, entropy weighting from Zhang et al. 2025) in a VLA-specific way rather than introducing new methods; 'self-speculative' framing is somewhat misleading
Modest speedup-to-FLOP-reduction ratio: 57% FLOP reduction yields only 1.46× speedup (~61% of theoretical), suggesting non-trivial implementation/hardware overhead not thoroughly analyzed

High hyperparameter complexity (Kglobal=30, Klocal=24, Kdynamic=20, τ, β, velocity thresholds, layer selection) with limited validation of generalization to new domains; velocity threshold formula (T = ⌊b + k·v⌋ + 4 with k=-1, b=7) appears arbitrary

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and limitations: LIBERO-Long (94.5%→93.4%) and real-world Transfer Tube (85%→82%) drops unexplained; no discussion of when spatial-temporal consistency assumption fails (rapid scene changes, occlusions, severe lighting variations)
Action-aware controller provides marginal improvements (96.8%→97.4% success rate, +0.3-0.4ms latency in Figure 8) that may not justify added complexity; could benefit from simpler fixed-K alternative

Design choices lack deep justification: arbitrary selection of layers 15 and 32 for global importance with no sensitivity analysis; entropy-based weighting computed once per task but Figure 5I shows entropy varies across steps, stability assumption questionable

Real-world evaluation limited in scope: only 4 tasks with 50-56 demonstrations each; single primary robot platform (Flexiv Rizon) weakens generalization claims despite appendix A.1.4 showing some cross-platform validation
EfficientVLA reimplemented rather than using official code, creating reproducibility concerns in baseline comparisons; FastV and DivPrune underperform significantly without adequate explanation
